sections.text:
When the Apostle gives thanks to God through Jesus Christ, says that through him we received grace and apostleship for the obedience of faith among all nations, or says that through him we have access to the grace in which we stand and rejoice, he sets before us the benefits bestowed upon us by the Son. At one time the grace of good things passes from the Father to us through him; at another he brings us through himself to the Father.

When Paul says, “through whom we received grace and apostleship,” he shows that the supply of good things comes to us through the Son. When he says, “through whom we have access,” he shows our reception and union with God through Christ. Does confessing the grace he works in us diminish his glory? On the contrary, the recital of his benefits is itself a fitting ground for glorifying him.

For this reason Scripture does not present the Lord to us under one name only, nor only by titles that directly indicate his divinity and majesty. Sometimes it uses names descriptive of his nature: Son, true Son, Only-begotten God, Power of God, Wisdom, Word. At other times, because the grace he bestows on us is manifold, Scripture gives him innumerable titles according to the needs of those who receive his goodness: Shepherd, King, Physician, Bridegroom, Way, Door, Fountain, Bread, Axe, Rock.

These titles do not define his nature. They show the variety of his activity, bestowed in compassion upon his own creation according to the particular need of each. Those who flee to his governing care and, through patient endurance, are corrected from their wandering are called sheep, and he declares himself their Shepherd, because they hear his voice and refuse strange teaching. To those who need righteous rule he is King. Because through the straight path of his commandments he leads people to good works and safely receives those who take refuge in him by faith, he is Door: “If anyone enters through me, he shall go in and out and find pasture.” Because he is a strong, unshaken defense for the faithful, he is Rock.

Among such titles, “through him” is especially clear when he is called Door or Way. Yet as God and Son he is glorified with the Father: “At the name of Jesus every knee shall bend, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” We therefore use both forms: one proclaims his proper dignity, the other his grace toward us.

Through him comes every help to our souls, and an appropriate name is devised for each form of his care. When he presents to himself the blameless soul without spot or wrinkle, like a pure virgin, he is called Bridegroom. When he receives a soul wounded by the evil blows of the devil and heals it in the grave sickness of sins, he is called Physician.

Do such acts of care bring our thoughts of him down to something low? Or do they rather fill us with amazement at both the mighty power and the loving-kindness of the Savior, who endured to share our weaknesses and was able to descend to our weakness?

Neither heaven nor earth, the vast seas, creatures of water and land, plants, stars, air, seasons, nor the varied ordering of the universe manifests the greatness of his power so much as this: that God, the One who cannot be contained, was able without suffering change in his divinity to engage death through flesh so that through his own suffering he might grant us freedom from suffering.

When the Apostle says, “In all these things we overwhelmingly conquer through him who loved us,” the expression does not suggest low or servile ministry but help exercised in the dominion of his might. He himself bound the strong man and plundered his goods—that is, us whom the enemy had abused for every evil work—and made us vessels useful to the Master, prepared for every good work.

Thus through him we obtained access to the Father, being transferred from the authority of darkness into the inheritance of the saints in light. We must not think of the economy through the Son as compelled service arising from servile inferiority, but as voluntary care for his own creation, working in goodness and compassion according to the will of God the Father.

Whenever the Lord is called Way, we rise to a higher meaning. We understand the Way as our orderly advance toward perfection through works of righteousness and the illumination of knowledge, always reaching toward what lies ahead until we arrive at the blessed end: the knowledge of God, which the Lord grants through himself to those who trust in him. Our Lord is the truly good Way, free from error and wandering, leading to the One who is truly good, the Father: “No one comes to the Father except through me.” Such is our ascent to God through the Son.

We should next speak of the way good things are supplied from the Father to us through the Son. Since every created nature—visible and intelligible—needs God's care in order to be held together, the creative Word, the Only-begotten God, apportions help according to the need of each. His gifts are varied because those who receive them are varied, yet each gift is proportioned to what its recipient requires.

He enlightens those held in the darkness of ignorance; therefore he is the true Light. He judges, measuring recompense according to works; therefore he is the righteous Judge, for “the Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son.” He raises those who have fallen from the height of life into sin; therefore he is Resurrection.

He accomplishes all things by the touch of his power and the effective movement of his will. He shepherds, enlightens, nourishes, guides, heals, raises, brings into being what did not exist, and holds together what has been created. In this way the good things from God reach us through the Son, who performs each operation with a speed surpassing speech, lightning, light through air, the movement of sight, and even the motions of our own thought.

What interval of time would be needed by the One who “upholds all things by the word of his power,” who does not act bodily or require manual workmanship for creation, but whose undivided will is immediately followed by the nature of things coming into existence? As Judith says, “You thought, and all that you conceived stood before you.”

Yet lest the greatness of the works lead us to imagine that the Lord is without origin from the Father, the One who is Life itself says, “I live through the Father”; the Power of God says, “The Son can do nothing from himself”; and self-complete Wisdom says, “I received a commandment what I should say and what I should speak.” Through all these he guides us toward understanding the Father and refers the wonder of his works to the Father, so that through the Son we may know the Father.

The Father is not contemplated through a separate operation different from the Son's, for “whatever he sees the Father doing, the Son likewise does.” Rather, the Father receives the glory offered to him through the Only-begotten and is exalted by those who recognize him as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, “through whom are all things and for whom are all things.”

For this reason the Lord says, “All that is mine is yours,” since the sovereignty over created things is referred to the Father, and “what is yours is mine,” since the cause of creating comes to the Son from the Father. The Son does not operate by borrowed assistance or by receiving individual commissions for each work. That would be the condition of a servant and wholly unworthy of divine dignity.

Rather, the Word is full of the Father's good things, shining forth from the Father, and does all things according to the likeness of the One who begot him. If he is without variation according to essence, he is without variation also according to power; and where power is equal, operation is also equal. Christ is “the Power of God and the Wisdom of God.” Thus all things came into being through him and were created through him and for him, not because he performs an instrumental or servile ministry, but because as Creator he fulfills the Father's will.

Therefore when he says, “I did not speak from myself,” “As the Father told me, so I speak,” “The word you hear is not mine but belongs to the One who sent me,” and, “As the Father commanded me, so I do,” he does not speak as one without free will or initiative, waiting for instructions to be issued. He makes known that his own will is united inseparably and without interval to the Father's.

We must not understand the Father's “command” as a verbal order imposed on a subordinate Son. In a manner worthy of God we should understand a communication of will, like the impression of a form, manifested timelessly from Father to Son. “The Father loves the Son and shows him all things”; thus all that belongs to the Father belongs to the Son, not acquired little by little, but present together and at once.

It would be absurd to imagine the Wisdom of God, Maker of all creation, eternally perfect, wise without being taught, the Power of God “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,” as needing lessons one by one to determine the manner and measure of his activity. If the Father's wisdom is infinite and the Son were always learning it in successive lessons, he could never reach perfection. Whoever denies that the Son has all things from the beginning is driven by the logic of the position to deny that he ever reaches completion.

“Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” This does not mean a bodily outline or shape, for the divine nature is free from composition. It means the goodness of will which, being inseparable from the essence, is seen as alike and equal—or rather one and the same—in Father and Son.

What then does it mean that he “became obedient,” and that the Father “handed him over for us all”? It means that the Son has from the Father the work of acting in goodness on behalf of humanity. Yet hear also that “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law,” and that “while we were still sinners Christ died for us.”

Pay close attention to the Lord's own words. When he teaches us about the Father he also uses expressions of sovereign authority: “I will; be cleansed”; “Be silent; be muzzled”; “But I say to you”; “Deaf and mute spirit, I command you,” and many similar sayings. Through these we recognize our Lord and Creator; through the other sayings we are taught concerning the Father of our Lord and Creator.

Thus the truth is demonstrated from every side: the Father creating through the Son neither makes the Father's creation imperfect nor indicates weakness in the Son's activity. It manifests the unity of their will. Therefore the expression “through whom” confesses the initiating Cause but does not accuse the effective Cause of inferiority.

translator_notes: Direct Mercy translation from Basil's Greek PG 32 text.
The chapter distinguishes the Son's voluntary divine economy from servile subordination.
The language of command is interpreted as timeless unity and communication of will between Father and Son.
